    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that skydance’s marketing division is the latest unit to reveal its new leadership structure. Following its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery in October, Skydance has been busy working to mesh the operations of the two media companies.

    Chief marketing officer Rebecca Mall, in a memo to her team, declared the upcoming vision for the marketing team. “We have an incredible opportunity to build a more unified, innovative and effective marketing organization – one that breaks down silos, understands our audiences better than anyone and harnesses the power of creativity, data and technology to set a new standard for our industry,” according to the memo.

    She added that the team’s job is not just to market what they create, but also to help drive growth and success for the entire Skydance manufacturer.

    Mall revealed that cross-company marketing and corporate brand, data & analytics, media, partnerships, and franchise and kids & family will now be housed under one roof. The new leadership team includes Annah Zafrani, who will be tasked with leading Skydance’s cross-company marketing and brand unit. Zafrani, who comes from Paramount Skydance, will coordinate priority campaigns across the media company’s businesses and lead corporate brand marketing. Reporting to her will be, also from the Paramount Skydance side, Katie Hutchings, svp, brand marketing, creative and strategy, and her team.

    Paramount Skydance’s Angie Sharma will lead franchise and kids & family, building one plan per franchise across content, consumer products, games, and experiences, with kids & family viewed as a key growth priority.

    Jamal Salmon, who comes from Paramount Skydance, will lead data & analytics for marketing, and will also report to Josh Goldstine, president of worldwide marketing & distribution, who will also be responsible for film marketing. Salmon will also have a dotted line to Hugh Williams, chief engineer and evp for consumer and monetization engineering; and Josh Walker, chief financial and strategy officer for direct to consumer. The DTC unit oversees streaming and video-on-demand.

    Paramount Skydance’s Michelle Hagen will lead brand partnerships, with Julie Moore, evp of brand partnerships, reporting to her, and Dana Nussbaum, co-head of global motion pictures marketing, Warner Bros., focusing on theatrical. Malene Sam, svp, originals, who was part of Paramount Skydance, report both to Hagen and Shauna Spenley, who leads DTC media. Under Spenley, Sam will be focused on TV and DTC.

    Finally, Seth Goren, who comes from WBD, will lead media, bringing together media strategy, media buying, and agency management across the company. He will report to Mall. But for theatrical media work, he also will report to Nussbaum. For his DTC media work, he will report to Spenley, and for his TV work, he will have a reporting line to Mike Benson, who leads TV Marketing.

    In a recent development, the realignment of the marketing team has led to the departure of Meg Maro, the global head of franchise. Mall thanked her for her contributions during her time at the firm.

    Maro concluded saying: “We have an extraordinary opportunity to redefine what marketing can achieve in our industry, and I can’t wait to see what we accomplish together.”.

    In a recent development, mark Mwachiro is a TVNewser contributor who has been writing for the blog since March 2022. Based out of Fresh York, Mark has also contributed to ADWEEK.

    Industry News: Anthropic indicates no to ads but Wall Street may have other ideas

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (855 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • Anthropic is a public firm now, which puts it on an unofficial path to an ads business.
    • Recent findings suggest that unofficial because the company’s official position is still firmly against ads.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Anthropic is a public firm now, which puts it on an unofficial path to an ads business.

    Recent findings suggest that unofficial because the company’s official position is still firmly against ads. It went as far as spending Super Bowl money on a campaign mocking OpenAI for bringing them to ChatGPT. Its prospectus, the document pitching those public shares to investors, leaves advertisers out of the business altogether.

    “Is it cynical to expect Anthropic to follow the same route? Not really. More like an educated guess,” said ad tech expert Shirley Marschall.

    Besides, the company has already left the door open, she continued. Its pledge rules out sponsored links adjacent to conversations, but in the same post it says it will keep building features that help users “find, compare, or buy products, connect with businesses.” And once an agent recommends products, retail media will pay to be in those recommendations, Marschall stated, before adding: “Let’s see Anthropic turn that ad revenue down,” she added.

    In a recent development, advertisers, for their part, will be watching closely, and with mixed feelings. On the one hand, a newly introduced media seller means a new platform to wrangle and one more set of tools and teams to learn at a time when most are still working out how to buy ChatGPT. On the other hand, Claude’s audience is also spending more and more time in those conversation threads. For marketers, that’s a hard place to stay out of for long.

    According to recent reports, “Anthropic, like any organization, has a stance towards handling consumer data and inadvertently how advertising is considered,” said independent ad tech consultant Jonathan D’Souza Rauto. “But monetization is a lucrative form of revenue. I’d expect Anthropic to have a change of heart. Look no further to how Apple has played this advertising game over the past few years despite being considered anti-advertising.”.

    It has been revealed that life as a public company isn’t cheap, after all, and it’s even less cheap for an AI company that has signed up for approximately $895.4 billion in compute and infrastructure commitments, some running to 2045. That’s more than 13 years of revenue at its current pace, given Q3 revenue of $17 billion. The revenue covering that bill is far less locked in since 80% of revenue is consumption-based and the S-1 claims many customers can cut usage or terminate on short notice. In fact, the company has already warned that “operating margins may compress when large tranches arrive.”.

    In a recent development, then there’s the free tier. “Free and promotional users may never convert to paid plans,” the filing admits, yet Anthropic still pays to serve every one of them. Analysts found that cost sits in sales and marketing out of sight of the headline margin. That arrangement holds as long as free users keep upgrading. If they stop, Anthropic is left with a growing audience it pays to serve and earns nothing from.

    OpenAI has already shown what that audience could be worth. ChatGPT ads reached a $1 billion annualized revenue run rate less than 200 days after launching. When both companies are trading, analysts will ask Anthropic why it’s leaving money on the table.

    “They’ll go after advertising, just not in the way some assume,” said Rob Webster, founder and CEO of TAU Marketing Solutions. “The prize for Anthropic isn’t ads inside Claude. Advertising is now a trillion-dollar market, and the real power sits with whatever brain coordinates it: deciding what runs, where, and why. That’s a far more valuable position than selling impressions. Anthropic wants to be a latest, better Microsoft or Apple. Selling tools to businesses. Not ad opportunities.”.

    There are reasons, though, why Anthropic may resist the lure of ads for as long as it feasibly can.

    Sources indicate that “Trust and impartiality really matter with LLMs, particularly among enterprise customers,” remarked Alex Tait, founder of Entropy. “In contrast to OpenAI, Anthropic is at the moment approaching operating break-even without ads suggesting its existing business model could be commercially sustainable without it.”.

    It has been revealed that anthropic’s anti-ads stance is based on its perspective that once ads become part of a business’s revenue targets, the pressure to maximize engagement can start influencing product decisions. For an AI app, in this case Claude, that creates a conflict: users expect Claude to help them make decisions in their own interests, not towards whatever generates revenue for the organization or its advertisers. And in its IPO prospectus, the company said that they want “Claude’s only incentive to be giving them [users] a helpful answer,” which is why they have “chosen not to introduce that pressure [ads] into Claude.”.

    Anthropic did not respond to Digiday’s request for comment.

    #89499. Future of Marketing Briefing: Consulting firms revive their marketing ambitions in the C-suite the holdcos covet

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2608 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Future of Marketing Briefing: Consulting firms revive their marketing ambitions in the C-suite the holdcos covet

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2608 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, join us Dec.
    • According to recent reports, this Future of Marketing Briefing covers the latest in marketing for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Friday at 10 a.m.
    • However the holdcos settle the question of whether the CEO route counts as due diligence, Deloitte Digital and Accenture Song got there first, and both have started selling marketing in the C-suite with a fresh push.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    According to recent reports, this Future of Marketing Briefing covers the latest in marketing for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Friday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →.

    However the holdcos settle the question of whether the CEO route counts as due diligence, Deloitte Digital and Accenture Song got there first, and both have started selling marketing in the C-suite with a fresh push.

    In a recent development, deloitte Digital’s offer is Converge, an operating system that strings together AI agents to run marketing and sales work, from research and briefs through to campaign deployment and deal tracking. Some of the agents are Deloitte’s own. Others are ones a client already runs elsewhere, and the whole thing plugs into the tools and clout contracts a brand is already paying for. Marketing and sales versions are live, with commerce on the way, and Deloitte pitches them as one front-office system tied to revenue, which it calls “brand to cash.” Because it’s sold as a license that stretches across sales, marketing and service, it needs sign-off well above the CMO, which suits a consulting firm that’s used to having those conversations.

    Sources indicate that accenture Song’s play in media, a market it has circled in the U.S. for years without committing. In September, it moved Melissa Fein, who built its media planning and buying business in Australia and Latest Zealand after leaving Initiative in 2024, to New York as U.S. media lead. This month it posted a job for a head of media strategy for the Americas. The ad describes a “new world media practice” with no legacy systems to protect, and asks for an AI-first strategist” to lead planning, build new tools and become the person senior clients call before a brief exists.

    In a recent development, candidates need hands-on command of econometrics, incrementality testing and attribution plus experience in big-spending categories like financial services, telecommunications, automotive and health. Those are the categories where the ANZ team won Australia Post and Mediabank. Accenture Song Ndidi Oteh has kept quiet on specifics, saying only that whatever it does in media won’t take traditional forms.

    “The real prize is the conversation before the brief,” remarked  Steve Boehler, founder of agency consultancy the Mercer Island Group. ”If you help define the business problem, design the operating model and decide how success will be measured, you are competing long before an agency review begins.”.

    Both plays echo what the holdcos have spent 18 months engineering: operating systems that run a client’s marketing for it and media businesses that sell more than buying. The consultants may have the better shot at making either one stick. They already sit with the CEOs, CIOs and CFOs who sign off on systems spanning sales, marketing and service and installing that kind of software is their day job. A holdco operating system, rightly or wrongly, still reads as an agency tool, built partly to make the agency cheaper to run. Accenture also arrives in the U.S. media with no legacy buying business to protect, so it can lead with measurement and tools before it has to sell buying power.

    Recent findings suggest that whether any of this translates is another matter. Consultancies have been trying to crack advertising for the best part of a decade, after all, and the media buying business still rewards a scale Accenture doesn’t yet have in the U.S. Then again, now is arguably as good a time as any for them to try, if not better. With Omnicom and IPG combined, substantial advertisers are down to three holdcos, and some are skipping the pitch one so a credible alternative has rarely been more useful. AI is also pushing decisions about how marketing works into rooms where the CFO and CIO sit, which consultancies have been in for years. And a C-suite that takes a closer look at marketing will start asking how agencies make their money, from data fees to principal media, which is an awkward question for any firm with a buying business to defend.

    “The consultancies may have an advantage in getting invited to design the system,” noted Boehler. “That is not the same as proving they can run marketing better. The client still needs evidence of better decisions, better work and better business outcomes, not just fewer handoffs.”.

    All of which makes the Publicis-WPP episode look a little quaint, partly because it was never quite the fight it was billed as. Sadoun spent months telling investors that Publicis was winning big accounts without a pitch. Rose, asked about it by an analyst, called it “this pitchless CEO handshake thing that I keep getting asked about” and said decisions that big deserve careful consideration. Publicis answered with an open letter treating that line as her theory, and the coverage did the rest. Somewhere along the way, a question about how clients choose agencies turned into a row about manners.

    What got lost was the shift both CEOs were describing. Major advertisers are increasingly buying data, identity and AI infrastructure, which a six-week parade of slide decks was never built to judge, so some now test one partner in depth instead of auditioning several. Those decisions are also moving up the organization chart, to executives who sign off on systems not campaigns. That’s how consultancies have always been bought. Deloitte and Accenture are built for long, technical evaluations run by CFOs and CIOs, and while the holdcos; remarks were being turned into a grudge march one launched a system that needs the c-suite’s signature and the other started building a U.S. media practice designed to win it.

    “Client CEOs and CMOs pay attention to CEOs of holdcos, especially when a transition in agency leadership occurs and the agency CEO conducts outreach to key clients,” stated Gartner analyst Jay Wilson. “But most recognize that while agency CEOs may set a direction for the agency, that direction may be slow to take hold – or never take hold – within the agency teams doing the actual day-to- day work. A strong relationship with, or aversion to, an agency chief executive is usually more consequential at smaller, independent agencies.”.

    Whatever gets agreed in the c-suite, someone still has to do the work.

    “The consultants don’t have to copy the incumbent model to compete,” said Boehler. “But they still have to do the work: plan, negotiate, deliver, reconcile and prove results. A different model is a proposition until clients experience the difference.”.

    Cinema admissions have climbed back on the strength of a fuller blockbuster slate and much of the ad money that shifted to digital during lockdowns stayed put. Most screens still sell their preshow through sales houses that have always sold offline.

    According to recent reports, mikkel Hagedorn, a WPP and Omnicom alum, has spent five or six years building a platform that lets buyers book cinema spots programmatically, target them against specific films and count impressions straight off ticket sales. The company is live in Denmark and Finland, where sales houses have handed it two minutes of a 15-minute preshow at a base CPM of around €75. Hagedorn’s bet is that exhibitors can bring cinema into the digital ad market while keeping the premium pricing newspapers gave away when they went programmatic.

    His company, called Cinemataztic, gives buyers two ways to purchase inventory: first, agencies already running programmatic campaigns can reach the inventory through supply-side platforms and demand-side platforms such as Smartclip Google’s DV360 respectively, which lets cinema sit inside budgets that were going to be spread across other channels anyway, Advertisers who would rather skip the intermediary fees can book directly through Hagedorn’s own interface.

    Sources indicate that either way, the buyer can pick what individual film they want to target, so a brand could run only against the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday movie if it likes. The impressions they buy come straight from exhibitors’ ticketing systems, which means one ticket sold counts as one impression. There are “no multipliers here,” stated Hagedorn, a dig at the audience multipliers that inflate numbers elsewhere in media.

    It has been revealed that so far a lot of the money has come from digital agencies edging up the funnel into brand work. Hagedorn said he has seen little cannibalisation of advertisers still buying cinema the old way. He said the business has grown 50% a year and forecasts the same for next year, when the manufacturer expands into Sweden, Thailand and a third, bigger market he wouldn’t share.

    Even so, the programmatication of cinema will be a slow burn. Advertising is still its third-largest revenue line after tickets and concessions. Most hand it entirely to sales houses on contracts of three to five years and only learn that demand is falling when the next guarantee shrinks. Hagedorn has been warning them about this for years. “They cannot stay offline forever,” he remarked.

    It has been revealed that brands that gatecrash cultural moments tend to stick to tournaments and royal weddings, and they rarely pick a game that lets players mug strangers in a fake Florida. Grand Theft Auto, the culture-warping franchise, is the exception, and its sixth installment is drawing the kind of guerilla marketing normally reserved for FIFA and the Olympics.

    It has been revealed that anyone trying to keep up can follow the running tally at GTA6Brands.com, an independent tracker run by Mike Litman that logs a new stunt each day for his GTA 6 Marketing News podcast. Hardly anything in culture still sets off that kind of scramble across so many brands at once, and with GTA the explanation is scale.

    According to recent reports, “I’ve tracked over 290 brand moves around GTA 6 so far, including around 130 unofficial activations,” noted Litman. “That’s a remarkable amount of marketing activity orbiting a product launch, particularly when so many of those brands have no formal relationship with Rockstar. What’s interesting is the range of brands getting involved.”.

    In a recent development, with media this fragmented, marketers have a shortlist of moments when a mass audience highlights up at the same time, and most of those moments involve a ball. GTA earned its spot on that list over 13 years. When GTA 5 launched in 2013 it made $1 billion in three days, which owner Take Two called a rate faster than any other video game, film or other entertainment product has ever managed. For context, Marvel’s “The Avengers” movie took 19 days to reach that number. In the years since it launched, the game has since surpassed 230 million units sold worldwide across three console generations. The wait for the sequel turned into an event of its own. GTA 6’s second trailer received 475 million views across all platforms within 24 hours of its release, beating the 365 million in 24 hours for Marvel’s Deadpool & Wolverine film. Take Two has issued $8 billion for its 2027 guidance for the fiscal year the game rolls out in. For a brand that wants a crowd all watching the same thing at once, that’s about as close to a World Cup final as entertainment gets, and nobody has to get past FIFA’s lawyers.

    In a recent development, “I think the fascinating thing is that GTA 6 has achieved something usually reserved for the World Cup or Super Bowl, but without the stadium, the broadcast rights or the traditional sponsorship machinery,” said Litman. “It’s become a cultural event in its own right. And brands aren’t waiting for permission to participate.”.

    Recent findings suggest that A few did get permission, though. Rockstar’s list of official partners is short and made up mostly of platforms. Sony signed an exclusive marketing deal, which put a “Plays Best on PS5” tag on the game’s official channels. Netflix got the “Extended Look” trailer six trailers before YouTube in August, in what Take Two boss Strauss Zelnick called a “groundbreaking partnership”. YouTube is running a 24-hour launch live livestream from its own channel, and the Miami Heat have redesigned court, custom uniforms and Vice City merchandise.

    “Nike is going back to its roots and what built the brand: cultural relevance through people who have the trust of a community. It is a bold choice when most advertising pitches are about AI. Nike uses AI too, as a tool, but clearly demonstrates it understands that what stays scarce is trust. Trust comes from identity and proximity: who is speaking, and how close they are to the community listening. It also shows what creators and athletes must build to ask a brand like Nike for more than just a campaign fee. Most of them are offering access to an audience that belongs to a social or tech platform, targeted and measured with the data that the platform makes available. Global stars aside, only those who directly own the relationship with their audience and their data can negotiate a share of the long-term value.”.

    — Alessandro De Zanche, founder of media consultancy ADZ Strategies on Nike’s bet on creators to drive growth.

    $70.7 million: The total amount that U.S. advertisers spent on ChatGPT ads during October.

    $83: The initial share price for Anthropic when the company went public.

    $24.6 billion: The total that U.S. B2B digital ad spend is expected to reach by the end of 2026.

    $1.65 billion: Total in pre-order sales ahead of the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto 6 launch.

    Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing people’ photosItaly has fined Meta €805m for scanning about 20 million Android users’ Facebook photo galleries without proper consent, and Meta looks to appeal, according to the BBC.

    Meta Testing Upcoming Prediction-Market App With EmployeesMeta staff are testing Takes, an internal prediction-market app where people bet points called “cred” instead of real money, and there’s no word yet on a public launch, per The Wall Street Journal.

    Inside YouTube’s Co-View PolicyYouTube now adds an estimated number of viewers watching on TVs to public view counts, based on a statistical model rather than device monitoring, though this doesn’t change creator payouts, according to The Publish Press.

    TikTok Outpaces Instagram on Brand Engagement Despite Equal Reach, Report FindsA Dash Social report finds that brand posts on TikTok and Instagram reach roughly the same audience, but TikTok earns a higher engagement rate by views (3.9% versus Instagram’s 2.6%), per Net Influencer.

    Substack job listing hints at a bigger advertising push in 2027Substack’s new payments job listing includes exploring ads around 2027, a clear change from its earlier “distant future” line on advertising.

    In Graphic Detail: Welcome to the agentic commerce quarterHoliday 2026 is shaping up as the first season in which AI shopping agents actually complete purchases, though it’s still early: only 31% of consumers say they’re likely to let an agent buy without reviewing the purchase first.

    Mail Metro Media’s next creator play is representing them Mail Metro Media, the Daily Mail’s ad sales arm, is building an in-house talent agency to represent its creators, which raises an obvious conflict between selling audiences to brands and getting the best deals for the talent.

    Inside Nike’s blueprint to turn creators into brand buildersNike mentioned it will give creators, local cultural voices, and everyday participants a larger role in building its brand, moving beyond major campaigns and superstar deals.

    With shareholders, an $895 billion compute bill and a costly free tier, Anthropic’s no-ads pledge may have a shelf life.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that coinMarketCap is hiring a Head of Research to turn CMC data into research that institutions, media and partners trust and pay for.
    • It has been revealed that CMC is the most referenced price and market data source in crypto.
    • According to recent reports, you will own our research agenda end to end: what we publish, how rigorous it is, and how it supports our enterprise data business.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that coinMarketCap is hiring a Head of Research to turn CMC data into research that institutions, media and partners trust and pay for. This is a senior, hands-on role reporting to the CMO.

    It has been revealed that CMC is the most referenced price and market data source in crypto. Our research already reaches millions each month through reports like our Monthly Exchange Report, Asset Watch and Market Pulse, and is cited by Bloomberg, WSJ, Forbes and Fortune. The next step is different. We are building CMC into a data platform for crypto, tokenized assets and broader markets, and research is how we prove the quality of that data to the people who buy it.

    According to recent reports, you will own our research agenda end to end: what we publish, how rigorous it is, and how it supports our enterprise data business. You will also be the senior voice on sensitive market analysis for CMC and its partners.

    Set and run the research roadmap, from recurring flagships (monthly exchange report, weekly market and asset coverage) to deep dives on exchanges, tokenized assets, RWAs and market structure.

    Build institutional grade research that showcases CMC data to banks, funds, data buyers and enterprise API clients, working closely with our API and BD teams on what buyers need.

    Own methodology and data integrity: define how we measure volume, liquidity, flows and reserves, document it, and make sure every published number holds up to scrutiny.

    Lead research on sensitive or fast moving market events, balancing speed, neutrality and accuracy, and handle review requests from partners with sound judgement.

    Be a credible public face for CMC research with tier one media, on panels and in interviews.

    Manage and develop a small research team, currently one research analyst, and use AI and automation to scale output without lowering quality.

    Partner with marketing, editorial and product to turn research into formats people actually read and share, from long form reports to charts and short social posts.

    7+ years in research or data analysis, with at least 3 in crypto or digital asset markets.

    A track record of published, data heavy research that institutions or serious media rely on.

    Deep understanding of market structure: exchanges, spot and derivatives, liquidity, onchain flows and proof of reserves.

    Strong quantitative skills and hands on data work (SQL or Python, APIs, large datasets).

    Excellent written English and the judgement to present sensitive findings neutrally and accurately.

    Experience leading or mentoring analysts.

    Background at a crypto data provider, an institutional research desk or a TradFi data business.

    Understanding of how data is packaged and sold to institutions (licensing, enterprise feeds, research subscriptions).

    Knowledge of tokenized assets, RWAs or traditional market data.

    Existing relationships with tier one financial and crypto media.

    Comfort using AI tools to automate data pulls and drafts.

    Mandarin, given our close work with Chinese speaking partners and media.

    • Recent findings suggest that most growth teams call themselves data-driven.
    • We want to be part of the 0.1%: a company where AI doesn’t just help the growth team, it runs the growth loop.
    • Then it’s your chance to define a latest category : The Operating System (OS) for Human Greatness Augmented with AI.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that most growth teams call themselves data-driven. They have a dashboard, an agency and a ChatGPT licence to write ad copy faster. That’s the 99%.

    We want to be part of the 0.1%: a company where AI doesn’t just help the growth team, it runs the growth loop. Every day, on every channel.

    Then it’s your chance to define a latest category : The Operating System (OS) for Human Greatness Augmented with AI.

    According to recent reports, science-backed. Design-led. AI-powered. Global.

    We’re not looking for someone who only advises on what to test, we’re looking for someone who builds it. A hands-on Head of Growth who can ideate, write the copy, design the strategy and launch experiments directly.

    Our growth machine has to be able to:.

    Sources indicate that 1. Generate hypotheses. Read the signals (ad performance, webinar attendance, sales calls, objections, churn reasons, comments, competitors’ ads) and propose what to test next, with a cost and an expected impact.

    It has been revealed that 2. Act across every tool. Not a chatbot in a tab: it reads and writes in our whole stack, from ad accounts to CRM, landing pages, webinars, email, social DMs and analytics.

    In a recent development, 3. Hold the full context of Paradox. Our DNA, offers, voice, member stories, past campaigns and what they taught us, in one shared tech giant brain.

    Sources indicate that 4. Ship its hypotheses. Produce the hook, the ad cut, the page, the email sequence or the funnel variant, and put it live.

    5. Measure with real KPIs. Every test is tied to a number that matters (cost per qualified lead, show-up rate, close rate, CAC, payback, LTV), not to likes or reach.

    In a recent development, 6. Learn and loop on its own. Scale what works, kill what doesn’t, write the lesson back into the brain, and launch the next cycle without waiting for a meeting.

    Sources indicate that this is already real. Our growth hub tracks every hypothesis and experiment, with its result. An ads library of thousands of creatives feeds our creative research. Agents cut ads from long-form content, prepare webinars, wire Instagram comment-to-DM automations and audit our tracking after every live. Athena, our AI coach, works with members every day.

    We believe self-help is broken: generic theory, a quick high, no real change.

    According to recent reports, we believe people deserve more. More than content. More than motivation.

    They deserve a system that knows them, one that adapts, challenges, and grows with them.

    Growth at Paradox means bringing people into something that actually changes their life, and proving it.

    - Human Intelligence (coaches, peers, and mentors).

    - Structured Intelligence (protocols, mental models, rituals).

    - Technological Intelligence (AI personalization, feedback loops, adaptive journeys).

    To create one seamless ecosystem: Paradox OS.

    Industry observers note that paradox was founded by David Laroche, a creator followed by over 2 million people and known for his interviews with icons like Tony Parker, Mike Horn, Richard Branson and Gad Elmaleh. We started in French. We’re building for the world.

    Sources indicate that here’s the bet: a organization that learns by itself grows in a way a company of people alone can’t. A small growth team running a self-learning machine can out-test, out-learn and out-grow teams a hundred times its size.

    Sources indicate that we hold ourselves to the standards of Apple, Spotify and MasterClass. While others hide their numbers, we let our results speak.

    According to recent reports, as Head of Growth, you’ll be the architect of a growth machine that learns by itself. In a classic growth team, people do the work and AI helps. Here it’s the other way round: agents do the work, you design the system, set the bar and make the calls.

    You don’t just manage a team, you get your hands dirty to identify growth levers and pull them yourself.

    ❌ The old way: a Head of Growth hires people and agencies, briefs them, and checks their work.

    It has been revealed that 🏴‍☠️ At Paradox: your team is mostly agents, and you build them yourself. You write their skills, plug them into our tools (ad accounts, CRM, webinars, email, analytics) and write the evals that tell an agent what "good" means: a hook that stops the scroll, a page that converts, a test that’s worth its cost.

    You give autonomy step by step: first an agent suggests, then it acts once you approve, then it acts alone within a budget and guardrails. You move each agent up a level only when its track record earns it.

    Industry observers note that example: in your first month you build the agent that reviews every ad set overnight. At first it only suggests. By month three it pauses losers and moves budget by itself within limits you set, and you only see what was decided and why.

    ❌ The old way: a media buyer checks the dashboards each morning, changes bids by hand and waits for the weekly report.

    🏴‍☠️ At Paradox: you build and improve the agents that watch every ad set, page, webinar and email sequence around the clock. They spot what’s dropping, find the cause, fix it or launch a variant, and report what they did.

    You give autonomy step by step: an agent can pause an ad on its own long before it can raise a budget. You decide where each agent stops and a human takes over.

    Example: show-up rate drops on Tuesday’s webinar. Before anyone notices, an agent has found the cause (a reminder that never went out), fixed it and started testing a fresh reminder sequence.

    ❌ The old way: a creative team briefs an agency, waits two weeks and gets five ads.

    🏴‍☠️ At Paradox: you build the agents that turn every live, interview and member story into hooks, ad cuts and shorts, that study what the best advertisers in the world are running, and that write in our voice.

    Your taste becomes the eval: you write down what makes a great hook, a great cut and a great story, in rules and examples the agents check themselves against. Each time you reject something, the reason goes back into the rules.

    In a recent development, example: one webinar becomes dozens of hook variants by the next morning. You keep the best few, and next week the agents’ first drafts are already closer to your bar.

    ❌ The old way: an analyst rebuilds the numbers in a spreadsheet at the end of the month, and nobody trusts them.

    🏴‍☠️ At Paradox: you build the agents that connect every touch to cash, from ad to lead, live, sale and transformed member, and that audit the tracking after every campaign.

    No number, no test: you define the KPIs that matter (CAC, show-up, close rate, LTV, payback), and agents refuse to launch a test that isn’t wired to one.

    Example: after each live, an agent cross-checks the ad platform, the CRM and our analytics, finds where they disagree and fixes the leak before the next live.

    ❌ The old way: lessons live in people’s heads and leave with them.

    Industry observers note that 🏴‍☠️ At Paradox: every result goes back into the tech giant brain, and agents read it before proposing anything. The machine never learns the same lesson twice.

    You measure the machine itself: tests per week, time from idea to live, the share of the work done without a human, and how many agents moved up an autonomy level this month. You push those numbers up.

    And always: no fake scarcity, no fake claims, real stories told with consent. The machine can scale, but it doesn’t decide what’s right. You do.

    Recent findings suggest that how you’ll know you’re AI-native: you spend your time building agents, writing evals and making calls, not doing the work by hand. Most experiments are generated and shipped by agents. The output grows every month while the headcount doesn’t.

    You’ll own these KPIs: LTV / CAC ratio, funnel conversion rate by stage, experiments debuted per week.

    Desired outcomes: conversion rates 2x better than baseline, growth experimentation that runs continuously, a predictable growth engine.

    Tools you’ll master: GA4, Optibase, Vidalytics, Clarity, Hotjar, Amplitude, Figma, Looker Studio, VWO, Optimizely, Claude Code, and whatever helps you see what others miss.

    You have ideally a minimum of 3 years of experience in Conversion Rate Optimization, Growth Experimentation, or Performance Marketing, ideally within SaaS, e-commerce, or digital product environments.

    You have a track record of designing, implementing, and scaling A/B and multivariate tests that have generated measurable improvements in revenue, user activation, or conversion.

    Sources indicate that you’ve built with AI and agents yourself: Claude Code, automations, APIs, evals, creative pipelines. Show us something you built, not a certificate.

    A Conversion Architect, skilled at diagnosing funnel bottlenecks and translating data into structured experimentation roadmaps that deliver measurable business outcomes.

    A Behavioral Strategist, fascinated by what drives human action, able to mix cognitive psychology, UX, and persuasion frameworks to design experiences that convert because they resonate.

    A Data-driven Creator, fluent in GA4, Hotjar, AB Tasty, VWO, Amplitude, not just running tests, but connecting insights to revenue, retention, and lifetime value.

    Loop thinker: you see every channel as a loop that can learn, and you can’t stop yourself from closing it.

    Taste: you know a great hook in two seconds, and you’d rather ship one great ad than ten average ones.

    In a recent development, numbers-honest: you say when a test failed. You care about real revenue, not vanity metrics.

    Builder, not manager: you’d rather build the system than coordinate an agency.

    Growth over ego: you love hard feedback, you read, study and learn fast.

    Cross-disciplinary: you move from psychology to spreadsheet to creative brief to code.

    Analytical: you turn a vague problem into a clear hypothesis, a metric and an experiment.

    English: Fluent English, you can hold a conversation on specific details with English-speaking colleagues.

    Our chosen language for written communication is English.

    ❌ If you need clarity before chaos — wrong place.

    ❌ If you prefer balance over intensity — wrong season.

    ❌ If you build to deliver, not to elevate — wrong mission.

    ❌ If you want to optimize without getting your hands dirty in landing pages, copy, or design — wrong role.

    ❌ If you want to manage agencies and budgets rather than build a machine — wrong role.

    ✅ If you’re obsessed with psychology, systems and creative….

    ✅ If you want to build the growth machine that learns faster than anyone else….

    ✅ If you dream of using AI to bring transformation to millions of people….

    Build one of the first truly self-learning growth machines, and write the playbook others will copy.

    Grow something that genuinely changes lives, with the proof to show it.

    Work with filmmakers, psychologists, engineers, and creatives obsessed with impact.

    You’ll compete with San Francisco companies.

    -> 🏅 Being surrounded by A-players who strive to perform.

    But you don’t just want a competitive paycheck, you also want….

    -> Playing a crucial role in the development of a firm whose content and products will be used by millions of people.

    -> Waking up in the morning feeling like you are making a difference is something!

    We receive messages every day from clients who have successfully lost weight, quit smoking, reached a milestone in their business, built better relationships, and made positive changes in their lives.

    But that’s not all, we believe that driven people deserve….

    -> 😎 A company culture based on autonomy & accountability.

    -> 🗽 Flexible working hours (but very hard working).

    -> 🌎 A remote culture from day one with the freedom to work from wherever you want.

    -> 🧍‍♀️ Standing desks paid by the company if you live far from our offices.

    -> 💻 Work on Mac, for us it counts :).

    -> 🏀 350€ per year paid by the organization to take care of yourself (for your gym, or dance class or whatever make you feel great).

    -> 📚 150€ of books or education - At Paradox, we are learner lovers and we want to support you in that.

    -> 🔥 Access to Athena - our Paradox AI Coach supporting you on anything personal or professional, we want you to live your best life.

    According to recent reports, ⚠️ To complete the recruitment process, each candidate must organize calls with his or her previous managers. If you are not comfortable with this : do not apply ⚠️.

    If all this sounds good to you, come and write the next chapter with us 🚀🚀🚀🚀.

    That job description resonated with you?

    Here is your tailor made hiring process.

    📃 A 6 to 8 minutes application survey (with a short video assignment).

    💻 A 30mn video call with Timy, HR, to deep dive into your career path and ambitions.

    💻 A 1h video call, to discuss how you’d fit into Paradox’s Growth team.

    💻 A 1h culture-fit video call, to assess alignment with our values and mindset.

    💻 A 1h final video call with David, CEO, to discuss the growth vision and the next milestones to build.

    💼 Reference check to understand how you operate across environments and help set you up for a smooth onboarding.

    Our recruitment process is tailored to do our best to avoid that you or us realize that we’re not a perfect fit. Every step serves a purpose and will allow us to get to know you better as much as it’ll help you understand more where you’ll be stepping in.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, we are hiring 2026 and 2027 Graduate Software Engineers into engineering teams around the world. As a global platform company we offer a wide range of software engineering challenges, in both open source products and commercial business systems. We have teams that work in a variety of languages, typically Python, Golang, Rust, C/C++, JavaScript and of course... Bash. We work from the very lowest levels of the Linux system - BIOS and boot loaders, firmware, kernel and drivers, all the way up to desktop applications and containers. We work on tiny devices like the Raspberry Pi and new RISC-V boards, all the way up to supercomputers, clouds and Kubernetes clusters. We work on compilers and toolchains, and we work on security, cryptography, performance and documentation. Some of our teams focus on packaging thousands of pieces of software, others focus on deep contributions to a single body of code.

    Industry observers note that if you are excited about the potential that open source has for humanity and the enterprise, you have outstanding results in your academic career, and you are excited to contribute to the open source stack, this is the best way to apply to Canonical. We will work with you to identify teams and projects that would be interesting and a good fit for your skills and motivations. The process is highly competitive, it will require effort and excellence to succeed if you apply here.

    In a recent development, most of our engineering teams work from home. We try to align a single team in a single time zone - EMEA (Europe, Middle East and Africa), APAC (Asia Pacific and Indian Ocean), and AMER (North, South and Central Americas). Even though you work from home, we try to ensure you always have colleagues alongside to coach and mentor you, and for the companionship of shared problem solving and pair programming. Larger projects have multiple teams and might span the globe. We work with the open source community and specialize in building teams that work well in the 'fishbowl' of open source engineering. This is full time work, five days a week, often solving hard problems with significant responsibility. We don't generally work weekends and nights and we do enjoy good holidays but we also expect productive and intense engagement Monday to Friday.

    In a recent development, we bring all our engineering teams together in person twice a year for a deep 'sprint' with other teams to stimulate discussion and enable a wide range of career development paths. This is a fantastic way to demonstrate and develop your skill in software, learn about a wide range of technologies, make a meaningful impact to open source, and see some very interesting new cities that you might never otherwise get to visit.

    If you find the open source stack amazing, and you have been a consistent high-performing student in your school and university, then this will be a challenging and exciting start to your career.

    Location: This is a Globally remote role.

    Recent findings suggest that we consider geographical location, experience, and performance in shaping compensation worldwide. We assess performance and revisit compensation twice annually to ensure we recognize outstanding colleagues. In addition to base pay, we offer a performance-driven annual bonus or commission. We provide all team members with additional benefits which reflect our values and ideals. We balance our programs to meet local needs and ensure fairness globally.

    Canonical is a pioneering tech firm at the forefront of the global move to open source. Our platform, Ubuntu, is very widely used in breakthrough enterprise initiatives such as public cloud, data science, AI, engineering innovation, and IoT. Our customers include the world's leading public cloud and silicon providers, and industry leaders in many sectors. We are founder-led, profitable, and growing.

    Powered by worldwide distributed collaboration since our inception in 2004, we believe tech and business leadership can emerge anywhere. We have no central headquarters. Most of us work from home, but we are exceptionally disciplined about this. We have very high expectations of all colleagues, and are champions of excellence. Working here is a step into the future and will challenge you to think differently, work smarter, learn new skills, and raise your game.

    We are proud to foster a workplace free from discrimination. Diversity of experience, perspectives, and background create a better work environment and better products. Whatever your identity, we will give your application fair consideration.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    What if your next playground was to build a global, iconic Brand, with a creative machine that never sleeps, and compounds?

    We’re not looking for a "Social Media Manager" to follow a calendar. We’re looking for an AI-native Creative Director (Brand & Content).

    Someone who understands that to win today, you don’t just need "content", you need a Movement.

    This isn’t another content job. Most content teams use AI to write captions faster. That’s the 99%. We want to be in the 0.1%: a media where AI runs the creative loop, from the signal to the hook, the cut, the post and the lesson. Every day, on every platform, in French and in English. You bring the taste. The machine you build brings the scale.

    Recent findings suggest that here’s the bet: a company that learns by itself grows in a way a company of people alone can’t. We aim for $10M in revenue with 10 people, each of them running a dozen agents.

    In a recent development, paradoxically, the more AI runs our content, the more human it has to feel. AI doesn’t make more of what everyone makes. It makes more of what only we can make.

    Our creative machine has to be able to:.

    Industry observers note that 1. Read the signals. Comments, DMs, retention graphs, saves, shares, search trends, objections from sales calls, and what the best creators and advertisers in the world are publishing right now.

    2. Hold the full context of Paradox. Our DNA, years of interviews, lives and courses, member stories, and every past post with what it taught us, in one shared organization brain.

    3. Generate in our voice. Hooks, scripts, shorts, carousels, cuts, thumbnails and captions, in French and in English.

    4. Ship. Format, schedule, publish and answer, on every platform.

    In a recent development, 5. Measure with real KPIs. Retention, shares, saves, follower growth, and the followers who become leads and members. Not likes.

    Sources indicate that 6. Learn and loop on its own. Double down on what works, kill what doesn’t, write the lesson back into the brain, and start the next cycle without waiting for a meeting.

    Recent findings suggest that this is already real. An ads library of thousands of creatives feeds our creative research. Agents cut ads from long-form content and wire Instagram comment-to-DM automations. And our product is AI-native too: Athena, our AI coach, works with members every day.

    At Paradox, we are convinced that greatness is trainable, and we believe self-help is broken.

    Most learning platforms are used the same way: consuming generic theories, getting quick highs, ending with no real change.

    People deserve more: a system that knows them, one that adapts, challenges, and grows with them.

    That’s why we want to empower people at scale, by leveraging cutting edge technologies like AI, and crafting user experiences with outstanding aesthetics.

    - Human Intelligence (coaches, peers, and mentors).

    - Structured Intelligence (protocols, mental models, rituals).

    - Technological Intelligence (AI personalization, feedback loops, adaptive journeys).

    To create one seamless ecosystem: Paradox OS.

    Paradox was founded by David Laroche, a creator followed by over 2 million people and known for his interviews with icons like Tony Parker, Mike Horn, Richard Branson and Gad Elmaleh. We started in French. We’re building for the world.

    You lead the Content Factory not by management, but with creativity.

    In a recent development, in a classic content team, people do the work and AI helps. Here it’s the other way round: agents do the volume, you design the machine, set the bar and make the calls. Humans do what no machine can: taste.

    Build a symbiotic strategy where David Laroche’s personal brand and Paradox’s company brand reinforce each other without cannibalization.

    Implement radical new formats (documentaries, conceptual shorts) that shatter the boring codes of the "Self-Help" industry.

    Define distinct, sharp editorial lines for each platform: Depth & Search for YouTube, Aesthetic & Vibe for Instagram, and Authority & Authenticity for LinkedIn.

    ❌ The old way: a strategy deck written once a year, and a calendar filled by habit.

    🏴‍☠️ At Paradox: agents watch every platform, every competitor and every comment continuously. They tell you which angle is rising, which format is tiring and which story our audience asks for. The strategy updates every week, on evidence.

    Take responsibility for the entire production chain from hooks to storyboarding the narrative, and ensuring the final cut matches the vision.

    Recent findings suggest that own the packaging: titles, thumbnails and the first 3 seconds. You test variants every week and know your click-through and retention numbers by heart.

    ❌ The old way: one shoot becomes one video and a handful of posts.

    Sources indicate that 🏴‍☠️ At Paradox: one shoot, one live or one interview becomes dozens of hooks, shorts, carousels and ad cuts by the next morning, in both languages. Concepts are tested with AI-generated drafts before we spend a day shooting them.

    It has been revealed that your taste becomes the eval. You write down what makes a great hook, a great cut, a great carousel and a great story, in rules and examples the agents check themselves against. Each time you reject something, the reason goes back into the rules.

    Act as the final quality check: nothing gets published if it doesn’t meet the "Paradox Standard" of aesthetics and storytelling, whether a person or an agent made it.

    ❌ The old way: a creative team briefs an editor, waits three days and gets two versions.

    According to recent reports, 🏴‍☠️ At Paradox: agents draft, cut, caption, translate and schedule. You keep the best, and next week their first drafts are already closer to your bar.

    Analyze retention graphs, CTR, and CPL to iterate based on feedback, killing what fails and aggressively scaling what works.

    ❌ The old way: someone pulls the stats at the end of the month and nobody changes anything.

    🏴‍☠️ At Paradox: agents read the numbers of every post every day, explain why it worked or didn’t, and propose the next test. You measure the machine itself: posts per week, time from idea to live, hit rate, and the share of the work done without a human.

    We started in French. You build the machine that takes Paradox to English-speaking audiences: channels, formats and voice that feel native, not translated.

    It has been revealed that and always: real stories told with consent, no fake claims, no fake scarcity. The machine can scale, but it doesn’t decide what’s right. You do.

    How you’ll know you’re AI-native: you spend your time on concepts, taste and calls, not on resizing, captioning and exporting. The output grows every month while the team doesn’t.

    Proven Content Builder: You have successfully grown a media brand, a YouTube channel, or a personal brand to significant scale (100k+ followers or millions of views). You understand the mechanics of virality and retention. You’ve created at least one format that broke out, and you can show its click-through and retention numbers.

    Elite Scripting Skills: You can show us scripts you wrote that performed. You know how to structure a narrative, write a hook that stops the scroll, and keep an audience engaged for 20+ minutes.

    Performance Fluency: You have worked in environments where content had to drive business results (ads, releases, conversion), not just vanity metrics.

    In a recent development, AI-native Creative: you’ve built content pipelines with AI yourself: Claude Code, automations, generative video, image and voice tools, evals. Show us something you built, not a certificate.

    It has been revealed that intolerant to Mediocrity: You have "Taste." You are physically pained by a bad font, a clumsy cut, or a weak headline. You fight for the details that others ignore, including in what AI produces.

    Psychology Obsessed: You don’t just "make content"; you study human nature. You constantly ask why people click, why they share, and what emotion drives them.

    OpenAI Getting Rid of Custom GPTs and Moving to Plugin Architecture

    📅 05 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (657 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • OpenAI has confirmed it will retire Custom GPTs and move the specialized workflows built around them to a new plugin architecture spanning ChatGPT and its Codex coding agent.
    • Custom GPT retirement is right now scheduled for Dec.
    • According to recent reports, for affected Enterprise workspaces, OpenAI's current migration schedule targets Oct.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    OpenAI has confirmed it will retire Custom GPTs and move the specialized workflows built around them to a new plugin architecture spanning ChatGPT and its Codex coding agent.

    Custom GPT retirement is right now scheduled for Dec. 11, 2026, although the company indicates timing and migration availability can vary by account and workspace.

    According to recent reports, for affected Enterprise workspaces, OpenAI's current migration schedule targets Oct. 26 for ending creation of newly introduced Custom GPTs. Qualifying Enterprise customers with approved deferrals can continue using them until Feb. 11, 2027.

    OpenAI has changed its UI to make GPTs less prominent, and when users choose to try creating a fresh Custom GPT, they are now prompted with an option to create a plugin instead.

    Rather than maintaining separate customized versions of ChatGPT, OpenAI is shifting customization toward plugins that can package reusable instructions, reference material, and connections to outside services.

    Under OpenAI's plugin architecture, a plugin can include one or more skills containing instructions and resources for repeatable workflows, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposing tools and external systems, or both. ChatGPT and Codex share a universal plugin directory, although some capabilities can remain specific to a particular environment.

    For organizations, that makes the change more than a simple renaming exercise. A organization could package recurring workflows into skills while using MCP servers or connected apps to give those workflows access to enterprise systems and data.

    In a recent development, openAI says creators will be able to migrate an existing GPT through the My GPTs interface. The GPT's instructions become a skill in the replacement plugin, while knowledge files are copied into plugin reference files and connected apps can be carried over.

    Not everything transfers automatically. Existing GPT conversations do not migrate, the selected model does not carry over, and Custom Actions may have to be rebuilt using an available app or a custom MCP server.

    In a recent development, sharing also changes. Migrated plugins start private, existing GPT customers do not automatically receive access to the replacement, and prior sharing settings do not carry over.

    It has been revealed that openAI is also cautioning organizations against assuming that migration will preserve behavior exactly. "A migrated plugin may respond differently," the manufacturer claims, recommending that users retest familiar prompts, reference-material use, required output formats, and integrations before relying on the replacement.

    In a recent development, that warning has contributed to pushback from some GPT builders, who argue that plugins do not fully reproduce the dedicated and predictable environment of a Custom GPT. Other complaints have focused on sharing, migration complexity, and differences in how migrated workflows use instructions and reference material.

    It has been revealed that despite those concerns, OpenAI is clearly consolidating around plugins as its common mechanism for extending its AI products. Its developer documentation now describes plugins as packages customers can "discover, install, share, and publish" across ChatGPT and Codex, replacing the separate-custom-assistant model with reusable AI capabilities that can be combined with enterprise tools and services.

    For more information, go to the OpenAI site.

    David Ramel is an editor and writer at Converge 360.

    Cisco has introduced Privileged Infrastructure Access, an approach to infrastructure administration that gives people and AI agents temporary, task-specific permissions instead of leaving standing privileges available after their work is done.

    According to a upcoming survey from identity security firm Delinea, 99.7% of IT and security leaders said their organization has a formal policy governing what data AI tools and agents are permitted to access. Yet only about 51% said AI access is checked against those policies in real time.

    Artificial intelligence is saving scientists significant amounts of time, but researchers are giving some of those gains back by checking the technology's work, according to a latest study involving Google, Google DeepMind, and MIT.

    Cloud Security Alliance's 2026 Top Threats report ranks identity as the leading cloud security concern, followed by two new AI-related risks.

    Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living.     We’re looking for a senior product designer to be the first dedicated designer on our product growth team, shaping how creators get set up, see value in their first days, and enjoy a seamless upgrade experience. Kit ships fast, and the product growth team builds the frameworks and systems that connect creators to the value in their blueprint as the product keeps changing. We need a designer who can balance rapid experimentation with long-term value for our creators.

    Product growth is a latest team at Kit, formed earlier this year. In the six months since, we’ve found our rhythm and started to move the numbers, but we’re still shaping how we work, how we prioritise and where we focus in the long term. As the team’s designer, you’ll be the design voice for growth, with real influence over how the team works and what it builds.

    You'll own the design of the moments that move our funnel: onboarding, activation, free trials, upgrade and upsell flows, pricing and checkout, and billing. You'll work in a team that learns by shipping, through A/B tests and ship-and-measure changes, and you'll use data to decide what to try next.

    This is a full-time IC role for a designer who loves connecting design decisions to numbers, moves promptly without sacrificing quality, and is excited about using AI to accelerate outcomes.

    We need someone who thinks deeply about user behaviour, interaction design and the product experience, and who is proactive about finding the next opportunity rather than waiting for a spec.

    You'll report to Dan Winer, Director of Product Design, and join a small, high-impact product design team at the moment consisting of four senior product designers and a senior design engineer. From day one, you’ll be part of the product growth team’s product trio alongside the product manager and engineering manager, shaping the team’s vision, priorities and how we work. You’ll also work closely with the team’s engineers.

    The Art, Science and Theater of Modern Marketing ft. Thomas Ranese

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • What if the best marketing advantage you have is something that cannot be replicated by an algorithm?
    • For Thomas Ranese, CMO of Intuit, it starts with theater, empathy and understanding what people are actually trying to achieve.
    • In this episode of Marketing Vanguard, Jenny Rooney sits down with Thomas to unpack how an unconventional career spanning theater, Google and Uber shaped his approach to marketing leadership.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    What if the best marketing advantage you have is something that cannot be replicated by an algorithm?

    For Thomas Ranese, CMO of Intuit, it starts with theater, empathy and understanding what people are actually trying to achieve.

    In this episode of Marketing Vanguard, Jenny Rooney sits down with Thomas to unpack how an unconventional career spanning theater, Google and Uber shaped his approach to marketing leadership.

    From growing up behind the counter of his father’s pasta shop to leading marketing at one of the world’s biggest financial technology platforms, Thomas gets into why emotional connection can be just as powerful as performance data.

    He also addresses why AI needs human expertise to earn customer trust, and why brands should bring more humanity, creativity, and purpose into modern marketing.

    Thomas Ranese is Chief Marketing Officer at Intuit, a global technology platform serving millions of customers worldwide with TurboTax, QuickBooks, Credit Karma and Mailchimp.

    His career has taken him through some very different worlds, including theater, consulting, government and nonprofit work, Google and Uber. His approach to marketing is rooted in a simple idea: understand what people are trying to achieve, then build brands and experiences that help them get there. He strongly believes in storytelling and using humor to make complex information more relatable.

    At Intuit, Thomas is helping shape the company’s evolution into an integrated, AI-powered financial technology platform, with a focus on combining technology with human expertise to help consumers and businesses prosper.

    07:18 Marketing Is Theater, and It Goes Beyond Advertising — Thomas breaks down the three different kinds of theater that shape modern marketing: the storytelling and drama of advertising, the emotions and interactions built into customer experience, and the immersive experiences brands create through retail. He also believes real-world human interactions will become increasingly crucial as more of our lives move into digital and AI-powered environments.

    12:44 What a Pasta Shop Taught Him About Customer Obsession — Thomas traces his interest in marketing back to his childhood, when he spent time working in his father’s small pasta shop. He loved being behind the counter, helping customers and figuring out what they needed. He even created his father’s first promotional newsletter on a Commodore 64. Looking back, he sees those early experiences as the foundation of his approach to customer connection, communication and service.

    16:01 Why AI Needs Human Intelligence Too — Intuit is building AI into the core of its financial technology platform, but Thomas is particularly focused on the role human experts play alongside it. When customers are making important decisions about taxes, credit or their businesses, getting the right answer matters. AI can provide powerful technology and efficiency, but human expertise brings verification, empathy and the confidence customers need to act.

    Industry observers note that 19:57 Money Is a Means to an End. So Is Your Product — Thomas challenges brands to think beyond what their products do and focus on what customers want to achieve with them. Small business owners aren’t necessarily starting businesses because they want to make money; they’re pursuing a craft, building a lifestyle, serving customers or creating opportunities for their families. The same principle applies across categories: brands become more meaningful when they understand the bigger ambitions their products help people achieve.

    22:00 Intuit’s Goal for Financial Literacy — Thomas explains how Intuit is connecting its mission to power prosperity with financial literacy education. Through Intuit for Education, the tech giant aims to reach 50 million students by 2030, addressing the fact that only 32% of students graduate able to pass a basic financial literacy exam. For Thomas, this is an opportunity to create meaningful social impact while building trust and introducing a new generation to the tools that can help them succeed.

    In a recent development, 26:02 Why CMOs Should be Fully Involved — Thomas pushes back on the idea that senior marketing leaders should step away from execution as their organizations grow. With technology and AI changing marketing so swiftly, he believes CMOs need to stay hands-on, understand the tools and continue learning. He argues that the bigger the organization, the more crucial this becomes, especially when it is easy to become disconnected from the actual work and the customers being served.

    Jenny Rooney is Chief Brand and Community Officer, leading strategy for the overall ADWEEK brand as well as the ways in which we serve and support our audiences with high-value content, products, partnerships and experiences, notably through our community programs such as Marketing Vanguard.

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Enterprise ambitions around AI are running into a fundamental problem: Orgnanizations aren't always confident in the networks those projects depend on, according to a report from telecommunications provider Arelion.
    • Recent findings suggest that the research found that concerns about network providers have caused organizations to rethink strategic initiatives over the past two years.
    • The findings come from Arelion's report, "The Trust Illusion: Why AI and Digital Transformation Need More Than a Reliable Network," based on a survey of 518 senior enterprise network decision-makers in the U.S., U.K., Germany, and France conducted by Savanta.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Enterprise ambitions around AI are running into a fundamental problem: Orgnanizations aren't always confident in the networks those projects depend on, according to a report from telecommunications provider Arelion.

    Recent findings suggest that the research found that concerns about network providers have caused organizations to rethink strategic initiatives over the past two years. Among respondents whose initiatives were affected, AI and data-driven projects were the most cited, at 49%. That put AI ahead of security and compliance programs at 44%, digital transformation at 42%, and cloud migration at 38%.

    The findings come from Arelion's report, "The Trust Illusion: Why AI and Digital Transformation Need More Than a Reliable Network," based on a survey of 518 senior enterprise network decision-makers in the U.S., U.K., Germany, and France conducted by Savanta.

    According to recent reports, all respondents worked for organizations with more than 2,000 employees and influenced network strategy across data centers, cloud, and connectivity. Of those surveyed, 66% had final sign-off responsibility. The results suggest that as organizations pursue increasingly data-intensive AI projects, confidence in the network infrastructure supporting them could become another deployment obstacle.

    On the surface, Arelion found little evidence of a trust crisis. A total of 93% of respondents noted they largely or completely trust their current network provider, while 83% said that trust has strengthened over time.

    The picture changes when respondents are asked about a serious network incident. Only 15% remarked they have complete confidence in their provider's ability to rapidly detect and address such a problem. Another 42% said their provider seriously lets them down anywhere from a few times a year to monthly or more frequently.

    In a recent development, those concerns have consequences beyond the network itself. Responding organizations have delayed, scaled back, or stopped strategic initiatives because of provider trust concerns, while others have added resiliency or risk-mitigation measures.

    AI and data projects were the most affected among respondents reporting an impact, as organizations try to move AI from experimentation into larger production deployments.

    A serious provider failure could also have substantial consequences. Forty percent of respondents said such an event would cause major operational disruption, while 18% anticipated significant financial loss or severe financial or reputational damage.

    Another tension runs through Arelion's findings. Enterprises need networks they can trust to support AI projects, but many of the same decision-makers are concerned about AI's growing role inside those networks. A total of 54% of respondents identified AI and automation in network management and security as the factors most likely to negatively affect network trust over the next three years. That ranked ahead of data sovereignty expectations and geopolitical instability, both at 39%, and regulatory requirements and quantum computing threats to current encryption standards, both at 38%.

    At the same time, respondents aren't rejecting AI as a network technology. Proactive AI-driven fault prediction was among the capabilities they stated would matter most to future trust, alongside stronger built-in security, greater accountability, and responsive support. That leaves enterprises in an unusual position: AI is increasing their dependence on digital infrastructure while also raising questions about how that infrastructure itself is managed.

    Arelion has an interest in emphasizing the importance of network-provider trust, and the survey reflects the views specifically of network decision-makers at large enterprises. Still, the findings point to an infrastructure consideration that can get lost amid the rush to adopt new AI models and agents. AI projects ultimately depend on the networks, cloud environments, data centers, and connectivity beneath them. If organizations lack confidence in that foundation, access to better AI models alone won't remove the obstacle.

    According to recent reports, "Trust is influencing which strategic initiatives move forward, how organizations manage risk, and which providers they choose to work with," remarked Mattias Fridström, Vice President at Arelion. "As businesses become increasingly reliant on digital infrastructure, enterprises are looking for network providers that can demonstrate transparency, accountability, and operational excellence, not just availability.".

    The full report is available for download here at the Arelion site (registration required).

    Cisco has introduced Privileged Infrastructure Access, an approach to infrastructure administration that gives people and AI agents temporary, task-specific permissions instead of leaving standing privileges available after their work is done.

    Sources indicate that according to a fresh survey from identity security company Delinea, 99.7% of IT and security leaders stated their organization has a formal policy governing what data AI tools and agents are permitted to access. Yet only about 51% said AI access is checked against those policies in real time.

    Artificial intelligence is saving scientists significant amounts of time, but researchers are giving some of those gains back by checking the technology's work, according to a new study involving Google, Google DeepMind, and MIT.

    Cloud Security Alliance's 2026 Top Threats report ranks identity as the leading cloud security concern, followed by two fresh AI-related risks.

    Bruce reveals why standalone media RFPs are disappearing, and what it really takes to design connected consumer experiences.

    He also addresses why brands need to move from channel-first planning toward operating systems built around outcomes.

    It has been revealed that bruce Williams is CEO of dentsu X North America. Here, his focus is increasingly on helping brands move beyond isolated media planning toward connected operating models that bring together data, content, technology and consumer experience.

    With more than 20 years in media, Bruce has spent much of his career working at the intersection of media strategy, integrated marketing, technology and organizational transformation.

    He also works with clients on AI-enabled transformation, agency interoperability and latest ways to turn data into faster decision-making at both global and local levels.

    01:26 The “Media RFP” Is Quietly Becoming Obsolete — Bruce indicates media RFPs rarely arrive as standalone asks anymore. Brands increasingly want integrated briefs that connect media with creative, experience, CRM and loyalty, or they want agencies to solve bigger transformation problems. So, the agency conversation has to shift from “Can you buy media well?” to “Can you help us operate better?”.

    Recent findings suggest that 03:13 Your Customer Doesn’t Experience Your Brand in Silos — Marketing may still be organized into separate teams, systems and channels, but the person receiving the experience does not care about those distinctions. Bruce argues that fragmentation remains one of the industry’s longest-running problems because disconnected structures eventually show up as disconnected consumer experiences.

    Industry observers note that 06:22 On AI: Build the System, Then Stay Scrappy — Bruce does not see AI transformation as a choice between massive infrastructure projects and quick tactical wins. He points to work with Heineken that combines long-term data and technology integration with practical tools like local intelligence agents that move competitive and market data directly into local decisions.

    08:51 Why Agencies Can’t Keep Saying “Our Way or Nothing” — For Bruce, the future of agency relationships comes down to interoperability and optionality. Closed systems create friction. Agencies need to work directly with brand data, technology and other partners instead of expecting clients to conform to one proprietary model. Openness is becoming part of the value proposition.

    Jenny Rooney is Chief Brand and Community Officer, leading strategy for the overall ADWEEK brand as well as the ways in which we serve and support our audiences with high-value content, products, partnerships and experiences, notably through our community programs such as Marketing Vanguard.
